tier_reason: zlib-ng discussion 871 ('2.0.0 Benchmark comparisons') runs the public deflatebench harness (github.com/zlib-ng/deflatebench) on Silesia-small.tar and lists Cloudflare zlib next to stock zlib at levels 1-9 in two runs (i9-9900K/GCC 4.8.5, Ryzen 9 3900X/GCC 13.3.0); all quoted numbers match. Measured by the zlib-ng maintainers, independent of Cloudflare, but no compiler flags are stated, so B, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: zlib-ng discussion 871, deflatebench on Silesia-small.tar. Aug 2025 (mxmlnkn, Ryzen 9 3900X, GCC 13.3.0): level 9 compress Cloudflare 0.476 s vs zlib (zlib-ng minigzip) 2.106 s (4.4x, derived from page data), decompress 0.031 s vs 0.099 s (3.2x, derived from page data); level 6 compress 0.308 s vs 1.149 s (3.7x, derived from page data). Mar 2021 (Dead2, i9-9900K, GCC 4.8.5): level 9 compress 0.544 s vs zlib with its own minigzip 2.760 s (5.1x, derived from page data), decompress 0.041 s vs 0.131 s (3.2x, derived from page data). Cloudflare output at level 9 is about 0.5% larger (6,404,085 vs 6,371,682 bytes).
corrections.caveats: GitHub fork of madler/zlib (default branch gcc.amd64). README marks it deprecated: Cloudflare is avoiding memory-unsafe languages, plans no further development, and recommends zlib-rs; the February 2026 commits are hardening fixes (NULL checks, inflate state zeroing). Its higher levels emit slightly larger output than zlib (level 9: 6,404,085 vs 6,371,682 bytes on Silesia-small). In the same 2025 run zlib-ng (0.546 s) and libdeflate (0.441 s) are as fast or faster at level 9 with smaller output. Not included in lzbench. The repo itself carries no benchmark numbers.

notes: Numbers verified on discussion 871. Fold question: it is a fork of the baseline (madler/zlib), not of the listed zlib-ng, and has its own independent evidence and distinct SIMD/CRC code, so it stands as its own entry rather than folding into zlib-ng; tag it deprecated. maintenance_status left 'active' by commit date (2026-02-25) although the authors announced no further development.

tier_reason: The well-known independent lzbench suite (public code, inikep/lzbench) lists fastlzma2 1.0.1 alongside xz 5.8.4 and lzma 26.03 on silesia.tar with gcc 15.2.0 on a single thread of an EPYC 9555P; all quoted rows match. Compile flags are not on the page (only implicit in the Makefile), so B, consistent with earlier lzbench-based verdicts. The README's 20-100% claim vs 7-Zip 19.00 is first-party, chart only.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 20% to 100% speed gain at the higher levels over the default LZMA2 encoder in 7-Zip 19.00, for a small ratio loss (two threads, Silesia, chart only). lzbench 2.4 single thread (EPYC 9555P, silesia.tar): fastlzma2 1.0.1 -8 compress 4.52 MB/s at 23.18% vs xz 5.8.4 -7 3.01 MB/s at 23.15% (1.5x at matched ratio, derived from page data) and vs xz -9 2.75 MB/s at 23.01% (1.6x, derived from page data); -10 3.38 MB/s at 22.96% vs lzma 26.03 -9 2.55 MB/s at 22.97% (1.3x, derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: Compression-only speedup. In lzbench the fast-lzma2 decoder (78.5-79.1 MB/s) is slower than xz 5.8.4's decoder (122-124 MB/s) on the same data; streams remain standard LZMA2, so they can be decoded with xz/liblzma. Matching 7-Zip's ratio needs double the dictionary size, which raises decompression memory. The README baseline is 7-Zip's LZMA2 encoder rather than xz itself; FXZ Utils is the xz-compatible wrapper. Dual-licensed BSD-3-Clause or GPL-2.0.

notes: Rows verified on the lzbench README. Added the matched-ratio comparison (-8 vs xz -7) and the decompression-speed regression to caveats. Metadata (347 stars, last commit 2026-09-12, dual BSD-3-Clause/GPLv2) matches.

tier_reason: The independent lzbench suite (public code, gcc 15.2.0, single thread of an EPYC 9555P) lists slz_gzip 1.3.1 -1 at 316 MB/s, 46.97% vs zlib 1.3.2 -1 at 89.0 MB/s, 36.45%; compile flags are not on the page, so B, not A. The README's own Core i5-3320M table is first-party.

corrections.claimed_speedup: lzbench 2.4 (EPYC 9555P, silesia.tar): slz_gzip 1.3.1 -1 compress 316 MB/s at 46.97% vs zlib 1.3.2 -1 89.0 MB/s at 36.45% (3.6x, derived from page data); also ahead of zlib-ng 2.3.3 -1 (196 MB/s, 44.41%) and libdeflate 1.26 -1 (202 MB/s, 34.68%). README (single core of Core i5-3320M, Silesia): slz 1.2.1 232 MB/s (gzip) to 293 MB/s (raw deflate) at ratio 2.12 vs zlib 1.2.8 -1 70 MB/s at 2.74 (about 3x; zlib's huffman-only and RLE modes reach 88 and 81 MB/s); output often 24-32% larger; 28-byte stream state vs zlib's 256 kB per stream.
corrections.caveats: Compressor only (decompression goes through zlib or another inflater; lzbench decompress figures are zlib's). Speed is bought with a much lower ratio (46.97% vs zlib -1 36.45% in lzbench), so it competes with zlib level 1 and LZ4-class use; stateless design suits many concurrent streams (HAProxy). X11 (MIT-style) license.

notes: Numbers verified on lzbench and the README; corrected the README zlib range (70 MB/s is zlib -1; 81/88 MB/s are RLE/huffman-only modes) and the memory claim to the README's wording. Metadata (34 stars, last commit 2026-09-27, X11 license) matches; widely used via HAProxy.
